topic: Technician privileges: bands, modes and power

notes.front: What are a licence's operating privileges, in one sentence?
notes.back: What the licence class allows: which frequencies, which emission types and how much power.
notes.explanation: The control operator's class sets the privileges a station may use, and the rules give them band by band.
notes.example: A Technician may use voice on 28.400 MHz but only Morse code on 21.100 MHz: same licence, different privileges per band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is an ITU Region, as used in the FCC band tables?
notes.back: One of three world regions the band tables are divided into; the 50 states are in Region 2.
notes.explanation: Band limits can differ by region, so US figures in this deck are the Region 2 column. Some US Pacific islands, such as Guam, are in Region 3.
notes.example: The 2 m band is 144–146 MHz in Region 1 but 144–148 MHz in Region 2, which includes the US.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is CW, in one sentence?
notes.back: Another name for a Morse code transmission.
notes.explanation: Except where the rules say otherwise, CW is allowed on any frequency the control operator may use (97.305(a)), and on some Technician HF bands it is the only mode allowed.
notes.example: Tapping out a call sign in dots and dashes with a key is CW.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is modulation?
notes.back: Combining speech with an RF carrier signal.
notes.explanation: It is how a transmitter puts your voice onto a radio signal. The carrier is the steady radio signal the transmitter produces before your voice is added.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain
notes.example: Speaking into a handheld’s microphone: the transmitter combines your voice with its RF signal before it leaves the antenna.

notes.front: What is FM (frequency modulation), in one sentence?
notes.back: Modulation that varies the radio wave’s frequency in step with the message; FM or PM is usual for VHF and UHF voice repeaters.
notes.explanation: PM (phase modulation) is its close relative: where the rules name frequency modulation, phase modulation is also acceptable.
notes.example: A handheld talking through a local 2 m repeater is using FM.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A04, T8A02; 47 CFR 2.201(c)(3); US Navy, NEETS Module 12 (NAVEDTRA 14184), Appendix I (“Frequency modulation”)
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is amplitude modulation (AM), in one sentence?
notes.back: Modulation that varies the strength (amplitude) of the radio wave in step with the message, such as a voice.
notes.explanation: It is one family of modulation; FM and PM belong to the other, angle modulation, which varies frequency or phase instead.
notes.example: AM broadcast radio works this way: the strength of the wave follows the sound.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 12 (NAVEDTRA 14184), Modulation, Appendix I (“Amplitude modulation”, “Angle modulation”); 47 CFR 2.201(c)(2)–(3)
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)

notes.front: What is a sideband, in one sentence?
notes.back: A band of frequencies that amplitude modulation creates just above (upper sideband) or just below (lower sideband) the wave’s frequency, carrying the message.
notes.explanation: The rules define a single-sideband emission as an amplitude-modulated emission with one sideband only (47 CFR 2.1), which is why a transmitter can send just one of them.
notes.example: A voice sent by AM on 7.2 MHz produces one sideband just above and one just below 7.2 MHz.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 12 (NAVEDTRA 14184), Modulation, p. 1-43; 47 CFR 2.1 (“Single-Sideband Emission”)
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)

notes.front: What is SSB, in one sentence?
notes.back: Single sideband: a form of amplitude modulation, and a voice (phone) mode often used for long-distance, weak-signal contacts.
notes.explanation: The rules write Technician 10 m voice as emissions J3E and R3E, which are single-sideband phone.
notes.example: A long-distance voice contact on 28.400 MHz is typically made with SSB, not FM.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8A01, T8A03; 47 CFR 2.201, 97.307(f)(10)
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is a digital mode, in one sentence?
notes.back: A way of sending data, such as text typed on a computer, by radio rather than voice.
notes.explanation: The rules call such signals data or RTTY emissions (47 CFR 97.3(c)).
notes.example: Typing a message that your computer and radio send as data, instead of speaking it, is using a digital mode.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D01, T8D02; 47 CFR 97.3(c)(2)
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is FT8, in one sentence?
notes.back: A digital mode capable of low signal-to-noise operation: it can work with signals barely above the noise.
notes.explanation: Working with signals barely above the noise is what makes it useful for weak-signal contacts. It runs as software on a computer connected to the radio’s audio output and input, and Technicians may use digital modes such as FT8 on 10, 6 and 2 meters.
notes.example: Two computers exchanging short FT8 messages through their radios are using a digital mode.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T8D02, T8D01, T4A04, T1B05
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is harmful interference, as the FCC rules define it?
notes.back: Interference that endangers radionavigation or safety services, or seriously degrades, obstructs or repeatedly interrupts a lawful radio service.
notes.explanation: It is the level of interference the rules act on; Part 97 uses the term when saying who must cure a problem.
notes.example: Like the difference between a neighbour's noise you notice and noise that repeatedly makes your phone calls impossible.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain

notes.front: What does it mean when amateurs are a secondary service in a band?
notes.back: They must not cause harmful interference to, and must accept interference from, stations of the primary service.
notes.explanation: Several amateur bands are shared with non-amateur users who have priority there.
notes.example: On 70 cm, amateurs must not interfere with, and must accept interference from, US Government radiolocation (radar) stations: exactly the duties of a secondary service.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is PEP (peak envelope power), in one sentence?
notes.back: The average power a transmitter supplies to the antenna line during one RF cycle at the crest of the modulation envelope.
notes.explanation: In plain terms, it is the transmitter’s power at the strongest moment of your voice or signal. Technician power limits (97.313(b), (c)(2)) are stated in watts PEP.
notes.example: A transmitter limited to 200 W PEP must not exceed 200 W at its strongest voice or signal peaks.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: On which amateur bands above 30 MHz do Technicians have privileges?
notes.back: All of them: 6 m and every higher amateur band.
notes.explanation: The band table grants every band from 6 m upward to Technician, General, Advanced and Amateur Extra alike.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

image.alt: Technician privileges chart. HF, 200 W PEP maximum: 80 m 3.525–3.600 MHz CW only; 40 m 7.025–7.125 MHz CW only; 15 m 21.025–21.200 MHz CW only; 10 m 28.000–28.300 MHz CW, RTTY and data; 10 m 28.300–28.500 MHz CW and SSB phone. VHF and above, every amateur band, up to 1500 W PEP (lower in some areas): 6 m 50–54 MHz with CW only 50.0–50.1; 2 m 144–148 MHz with CW only 144.0–144.1; 1.25 m 219–220 (data only) and 222–225 MHz; 70 cm 420–450 MHz; 33 cm 902–928 MHz; 23 cm 1240–1300 MHz; 13 cm and higher.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from 47 CFR 97.301, 97.305, 97.307(f)(9)–(10) and 97.313 (eCFR as of 2026-09-22)

notes.front: What are the limits of the 6 m band in the US?
notes.back: 50 to 54 MHz.
notes.explanation: So 52.525 MHz is in the 6 m band; 49.00 MHz is just below it.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What are the limits of the 2 m band in the US?
notes.back: 144 to 148 MHz.
notes.explanation: So 146.52 MHz is in the 2 m band. (Region 1 stops at 146 MHz.)
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What are the limits of the 1.25 m band in the US?
notes.explanation: 219–220 MHz is for data only. So 222.15 MHz is in the 1.25 m band, not the 2 m band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What are the limits of the 70 cm band in the US?
notes.back: 420 to 450 MHz.
notes.explanation: It is a UHF band, where amateurs must not interfere with, and must accept interference from, Government radiolocation (radar) stations.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What are the US limits of the 33 cm and 23 cm bands?
notes.explanation: Both are UHF bands open to Technicians, like every amateur band above 30 MHz.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the Technician segment of the 80 m band?
notes.back: 3.525 to 3.600 MHz, CW only.
notes.explanation: One of four Technician HF segments; on 80, 40 and 15 m Technicians may only send Morse code.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the Technician segment of the 40 m band?
notes.back: 7.025 to 7.125 MHz, CW only.
notes.explanation: One of four Technician HF segments; on 80, 40 and 15 m Technicians may only send Morse code.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the Technician segment of the 15 m band?
notes.back: 21.025 to 21.200 MHz, CW only.
notes.explanation: One of four Technician HF segments; on 80, 40 and 15 m Technicians may only send Morse code.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the Technician segment of the 10 m band?
notes.explanation: The only Technician HF segment with more than CW: data from 28.0 to 28.3 MHz, SSB voice from 28.3 to 28.5 MHz.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

image.alt: Technician privileges chart. HF, 200 W PEP maximum: 80 m 3.525–3.600 MHz CW only; 40 m 7.025–7.125 MHz CW only; 15 m 21.025–21.200 MHz CW only; 10 m 28.000–28.300 MHz CW, RTTY and data; 10 m 28.300–28.500 MHz CW and SSB phone. VHF and above, every amateur band, up to 1500 W PEP (lower in some areas): 6 m 50–54 MHz with CW only 50.0–50.1; 2 m 144–148 MHz with CW only 144.0–144.1; 1.25 m 219–220 (data only) and 222–225 MHz; 70 cm 420–450 MHz; 33 cm 902–928 MHz; 23 cm 1240–1300 MHz; 13 cm and higher.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from 47 CFR 97.301, 97.305, 97.307(f)(9)–(10) and 97.313 (eCFR as of 2026-09-22)

notes.front: Where on 10 m may Technicians use phone, and with what emissions?
notes.back: 28.300 to 28.500 MHz, SSB only (J3E and R3E).
notes.explanation: Technicians may send only CW or SSB phone there; the 28.0–28.3 MHz part is for CW and data.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: On which HF bands do Technicians have phone privileges?
notes.back: The 10 m band only.
notes.explanation: On 80, 40 and 15 m Technicians are limited to CW.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Where may a Technician use digital modes such as FT8?
notes.back: On 10 m (28.0–28.3 MHz), 6 m, 2 m and every higher band.
notes.explanation: Data is authorized in 28.0–28.3 MHz, from 50.1 MHz on 6 m, from 144.1 MHz on 2 m, and on the higher bands.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Which VHF segments are limited to CW only?
notes.explanation: Other emissions on 6 m start at 50.1 MHz and on 2 m at 144.1 MHz; CW is allowed almost everywhere else too.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Where may SSB phone be used on the amateur bands above 50 MHz?
notes.back: In at least some segment of every band.
notes.explanation: Every band from 6 m upward has a segment authorized for phone, and SSB is a phone emission.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: In a band where amateurs are secondary, what must US amateurs do?
notes.back: Expect non-amateur stations there, and avoid interfering with them.
notes.explanation: A secondary service must not cause harmful interference to, and must accept interference from, the primary service.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Why should you not transmit exactly at a band or sub-band edge?
notes.back: Frequency display calibration error, transmitter drift, and sidebands could put part of your signal outside the band.
notes.explanation: Emissions from modulation must stay inside the band or segment available to the control operator.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Which US licensees may contact the International Space Station on VHF?
notes.back: Any amateur with a Technician class or higher licence.
notes.explanation: Space stations may use 144–146 MHz, which is inside the 2 m band that Technicians hold; no NASA approval is required.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the maximum power for Technicians on their HF segments?
notes.back: 200 W PEP.
notes.explanation: The limit applies on 3.525–3.60, 7.025–7.125, 21.025–21.20 and 28.0–28.5 MHz when the control operator is a Technician.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Except for specific restrictions, what is the maximum power for Technicians above 30 MHz?
notes.explanation: That is the absolute limit for every amateur station; some areas and bands have lower limits.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Where, above 30 MHz, does a lower limit than 1500 W PEP apply?
notes.back: 50 W PEP on 70 cm in certain military areas, on 33 cm near White Sands, and on 219–220 MHz; 10 W PEP for spread-spectrum.
notes.explanation: These are among the “specific restrictions” behind the 1500 W figure (97.313(f), (g), (h), (j)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Beyond the maximum, what power must an amateur station use?
notes.back: The minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications.
notes.explanation: The maximum is only a ceiling: the rule (97.313(a)) asks for the least power that gets the message through, whatever the limit on that band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Apart from emergencies, when may a Technician be control operator in an Amateur Extra-only segment?
notes.back: At no time.
notes.explanation: The control operator's own class sets the privileges; being designated by an Extra licensee does not change that.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: May a Technician make an SSB voice contact on 28.400 MHz?
notes.back: Yes: 28.300–28.500 MHz is open to Technician SSB phone.
notes.explanation: Keep power at or below 200 W PEP there.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: May a Technician make a voice contact on 21.100 MHz?
notes.back: No. On 15 m (21.025–21.200 MHz) Technicians may send CW only.
notes.explanation: Only 10 m gives Technicians HF phone.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: A Technician runs 300 W PEP on 28.350 MHz. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. The Technician limit on 10 m is 200 W PEP.
notes.explanation: The 1500 W PEP limit applies above 30 MHz, not on HF.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: A Technician runs 500 W PEP on 146 MHz, in an area with no special limits. Is that allowed?
notes.back: Yes. Above 30 MHz the limit is 1500 W PEP, barring specific restrictions.
notes.explanation: Still use only the minimum power necessary for the contact.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: May a Technician send FM voice on 50.050 MHz?
notes.back: No: 50.0–50.1 MHz is CW only.
notes.explanation: Phone on 6 m starts at 50.1 MHz.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Which band is 146.52 MHz in, and may a Technician use it?
notes.back: The 2 m band (144–148 MHz); yes, Technicians have all bands above 30 MHz.
notes.explanation: It lies above the CW-only segment (144.0–144.1 MHz), so phone is allowed.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Which band is 52.525 MHz in?
notes.back: The 6 m band (50–54 MHz).
notes.explanation: The 6 m band runs from 50 to 54 MHz, and 52.525 MHz falls inside it; it is a VHF band, open to Technicians.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: On 70 cm you hear a Government radiolocation (radar) station on your frequency. What must you do?
notes.back: Avoid interfering with it and accept its interference, as the rules require of amateurs on 70 cm.
notes.explanation: On 70 cm, amateur stations must not cause harmful interference to Government radiolocation stations.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: You want to call on 28.300 MHz, the exact bottom of the Technician phone segment. What should you do?
notes.back: Move a little inside the segment, so your sidebands, drift and calibration error stay inside it.
notes.explanation: Emissions resulting from modulation must be confined to the segment available to you.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Which of the following frequency ranges are available for phone operation by Technician licensees?
notes.back: 28.300 MHz to 28.500 MHz
notes.choices:
A) 28.050 MHz to 28.150 MHz
B) 28.100 MHz to 28.300 MHz
C) 28.300 MHz to 28.500 MHz
D) 28.500 MHz to 28.600 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: these are below the phone segment, in the CW and data part of 10 m. D: above the Technician segment, which ends at 28.500 MHz.
notes.explanation: Technician 10 m phone is 28.300 to 28.500 MHz, and only SSB phone is allowed there (47 CFR 97.305(c), 97.307(f)(10)); below 28.300 MHz is for CW and data.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which of the following U.S. amateur radio operators are allowed to contact the International Space Station (ISS) on VHF bands?
notes.back: Any amateur with a Technician class or higher license
notes.choices:
A) Only amateurs with a General class or higher license
B) Any amateur with a Technician class or higher license
C) Only amateurs with a General class or higher license, and NASA approval
D) Any amateurs with a Technician class or higher license, and NASA approval
notes.choicesExplained: A: General is not required; Technicians hold 2 m, where the space-station segment 144–146 MHz lies. C, D: no NASA approval is required.
notes.explanation: Space stations may use 144–146 MHz, in the 2 m band (97.207(c)), and 2 m is open to every Technician (97.301(a)), so no higher class or special approval is needed.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which frequency is in the 6-meter amateur band?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 49.00 MHz is below the 6 m band. C: 28.50 MHz is in 10 m. D: 222.15 MHz is in 1.25 m.
notes.explanation: The 6 m band is 50–54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz is inside it. (47 CFR 97.301(a))
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which amateur band includes 146.52 MHz?
notes.back: 2 meters
notes.choices:
A) 6 meters
B) 20 meters
C) 70 centimeters
D) 2 meters
notes.choicesExplained: A: 6 m is 50–54 MHz. B: 20 m is an HF band (14.000–14.350 MHz). C: 70 cm is 420–450 MHz.
notes.explanation: Bands are named after their approximate wavelength, not their frequency limits, so placing a frequency takes converting it to the range the rules set for that band; 146.52 MHz falls inside the 144–148 MHz allocation for 2 m. (47 CFR 97.301(a))
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which of the following bands include frequencies where Technicians are authorized to use digital modes such as FT8?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) 10 meters
B) 6 meters
C) 2 meters
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B, C: each is correct on its own, so choosing one is incomplete.
notes.explanation: Technicians may use data such as FT8 on 10 m (28.0–28.3 MHz), 6 m and 2 m. (47 CFR 97.301, 97.305)
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: On which HF bands does a Technician class operator have phone privileges?
notes.back: 10-meter band only
notes.choices:
A) None
B) 10-meter band only
C) 80-meter, 40-meter, 15-meter, and 10-meter bands
D) 30-meter band only
notes.choicesExplained: A: Technicians do have HF phone, on 10 m. C: 80, 40 and 15 m are CW only for Technicians. D: Technicians have no 30 m privileges.
notes.explanation: On HF, Technicians may only send CW, except on 10 m, where SSB phone (emissions J3E and R3E) is also allowed (47 CFR 97.307(f)(9)–(10)).
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Which of the following VHF/UHF band segments are limited to CW only?
notes.back: 50.0 MHz to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 MHz to 144.1 MHz
notes.choices:
A) 50.0 MHz to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 MHz to 144.1 MHz
B) 219 MHz to 220 MHz and 420.0 MHz to 420.1 MHz
C) 902.0 MHz to 902.1 MHz
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B, C: these segments are not limited to CW. D: only A is correct.
notes.explanation: On 6 m and 2 m, phone and data start at 50.1 and 144.1 MHz, so the bottom 100 kHz of each is CW only. (47 CFR 97.305(a), (c))
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: How are US amateurs restricted in segments of bands where the Amateur Radio Service is secondary?
notes.back: U.S. amateurs may find non-amateur stations in those segments, and must avoid interfering with them
notes.choices:
A) U.S. amateurs may find non-amateur stations in those segments, and must avoid interfering with them
B) U.S. amateurs must give foreign amateur stations priority in those segments
C) International communications are not permitted in those segments
D) Digital transmissions are not permitted in those segments
notes.choicesExplained: B: no priority is owed to foreign amateurs. C, D: being secondary does not ban international or digital transmissions.
notes.explanation: A secondary service must avoid harmful interference to primary users and accept interference from them. (47 CFR 97.303)
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Why should you not set your transmit frequency to be exactly at the edge of an amateur band or sub-band?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) To allow for calibration error in the transmitter frequency display
B) So that modulation sidebands do not extend beyond the band edge
C) To allow for transmitter frequency drift
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B, C: each is a reason on its own, so choosing one is incomplete.
notes.explanation: Calibration error, drift and modulation sidebands can all push part of a signal past the band edge. (47 CFR 97.101(a), 97.301(a-e); see 97.307(b))
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Where may SSB phone be used in amateur bands above 50 MHz?
notes.back: In at least some segment of all these bands
notes.choices:
A) Only in sub-bands allocated to General class or higher licensees
B) Only on repeaters
C) In at least some segment of all these bands
D) On any band if the power is limited to 25 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A: Technicians may use SSB in these bands too. B: SSB is not limited to repeaters. D: no rule makes SSB legal on any band just because power is kept to 25 watts.
notes.explanation: Every amateur band above 50 MHz has at least some segment where phone, including SSB, is allowed. (47 CFR 97.305(c))
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: What is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators in their HF band segments?
notes.back: 200 watts
notes.choices:
A) 200 watts
B) 100 watts
C) 50 watts
D) 10 watts
notes.choicesExplained: B, C, D: lower than the rule; the Technician HF limit is 200 W PEP.
notes.explanation: Technicians may run up to 200 W PEP on their HF segments. (47 CFR 97.313)
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: Except for some specific restrictions, what is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators using frequencies above 30 MHz?
notes.back: 1500 watts
notes.choices:
A) 50 watts
B) 100 watts
C) 500 watts
D) 1500 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A: 50 W PEP applies only in special cases (some areas, and 219–220 MHz), not generally. B, C: lower than the general limit.
notes.explanation: Above 30 MHz, barring specific restrictions, the limit is the general maximum of 1500 W PEP. (47 CFR 97.313(b))
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: When, other than during an emergency, may a Technician class licensee be the control operator of a station operating in an Amateur Extra Class band segment?
notes.back: At no time
notes.choices:
A) At no time
B) When designated as the control operator by an Amateur Extra Class licensee
C) As part of a multi-operator contest team
D) When using a club station whose trustee holds an Amateur Extra Class license
notes.choicesExplained: B, C, D: a designation, a contest team or a club trustee's class never extends the control operator's own privileges.
notes.explanation: A station may only be operated within the privileges of the control operator’s own class (97.105(b)). Amateur Extra segments are outside a Technician’s privileges, so no designation makes it lawful.
notes.sourceLicence: A · public domain

notes.front: On 10 m, which is the Technician phone segment: 28.000–28.500 or 28.300–28.500 MHz?
notes.back: 28.300–28.500 MHz. 28.000–28.500 MHz is the whole Technician 10 m segment.
notes.explanation: The lower part, 28.000–28.300 MHz, is for CW and data.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Technician power: which limit is 200 W PEP and which 1500 W PEP?
notes.back: 200 W PEP on the Technician HF segments; 1500 W PEP above 30 MHz, barring specific restrictions.
notes.explanation: Mixing these two up is a common trap: HF is the lower limit.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: On Technician HF segments, where is CW the only mode, and where is SSB allowed?
notes.back: CW only on 80, 40 and 15 m; SSB phone only on 10 m, 28.300–28.500 MHz.
notes.explanation: CW is allowed on all four Technician HF segments; 10 m is the only one where Technicians may also use phone (97.307(f)(9)–(10)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)
